results.title: Parcels, Compiled from Opt-In Open Data Counties, Minnesota
results.description:
This dataset is a compilation of county parcel data from Minnesota counties that have opted-in for their parcel data to be included in this dataset. It includes the following 59 counties that have opted-in as of the publication date of this dataset: Aitkin County, Anoka County, Becker County, Benton County, Big Stone County, Carlton County, Carver County, Cass County, Chippewa County, Chisago County, Clay County, Clearwater County, Cook County, Crow Wing County, Dakota County, Douglas County, Fillmore County, Grant County, Hennepin County, Houston County, Isanti County, Itasca County, Jackson County, Koochiching County, Lac qui Parle County, Lake County, Lake of the Woods County, Lyon County, Marshall County, McLeod County, Mille Lacs County, Morrison County, Mower County, Murray County, Norman County, Olmsted County, Otter Tail County, Pennington County, Pipestone County, Polk County, Pope County, Ramsey County, Red Lake County, Renville County, Rice County, Scott County, Sherburne County, St. Louis County, Stearns County, Steele County, Stevens County, Traverse County, Wabasha County, Waseca County, Washington County, Wilkin County, Winona County, Wright County, and Yellow Medicine County. If you represent a county not included in this dataset and would like to opt-in, please contact Heather Albrecht (Heather.Albrecht@hennepin.us), co-chair of the Minnesota Geospatial Advisory Council (GAC)’s Parcels and Land Records Committee's Open Data Subcommittee. County parcel data does not need to be in the GAC parcel data standard to be included. MnGeo will map the county fields to the GAC standard. County parcel data records have been assembled into a single dataset with a common coordinate system (UTM Zone 15) and common attribute schema. The county parcel data attributes have been mapped to the GAC parcel data standard for Minnesota: https://www.mngeo.state.mn.us/committee/standards/parcel_attrib/parcel_attrib.html This compiled parcel dataset was created using Python code developed by Minnesota state agency GIS professionals, and represents a best effort to map individual county source file attributes into the common attribute schema of the GAC parcel data standard. The attributes from counties are mapped to the most appropriate destination column. In some cases, the county source files included attributes that were not mapped to the GAC standard. Additionally, some county attribute fields were parsed and mapped to multiple GAC standard fields, such as a single line address. Each quarter, MnGeo provides a text file to counties that shows how county fields are mapped to the GAC standard. Additionally, this text file shows the fields that are not mapped to the standard and those that are parsed. If a county shares changes to how their data should be mapped, MnGeo updates the compilation. If you represent a county and would like to update how MnGeo is mapping your county attribute fields to this compiled dataset, please contact us. This dataset is a snapshot of parcel data, and the source date of the county data may vary. Users should consult County websites to see the most up-to-date and complete parcel data. There have been recent changes in date/time fields, and their processing, introduced by our software vendor. In some cases, this has resulted in date fields being empty. We are aware of the issue and are working to correct it for future parcel data releases. The State of Minnesota makes no representation or warranties, express or implied, with respect to the use or reuse of data provided herewith, regardless of its format or the means of its transmission. THE DATA IS PROVIDED “AS IS” WITH NO GUARANTEE OR REPRESENTATION ABOUT THE ACCURACY, CURRENCY, SUITABILITY, PERFORMANCE, MECHANTABILITY, RELIABILITY OR FITINESS OF THIS DATA FOR ANY PARTICULAR PURPOSE. This dataset is NOT suitable for accurate boundary determination. Contact a licensed land surveyor if you have questions about boundary determinations. DOWNLOAD NOTES: This dataset is only provided in Esri File Geodatabase and OGC GeoPackage formats. A shapefile is not available because the size of the dataset exceeds the limit for that format. The distribution version of the fgdb is compressed to help reduce the data footprint. QGIS users should consider using the Geopackage format for better results.As of 09/02/2026, updates were made to fix standardization issues with St. Louis County state pin field and Murray County owner name field.

results.title: Government-Owned Lands, Derived from Opt-In Open Data Counties, Minnesota
results.description:
This dataset is a subset of the statewide parcel dataset. The parcels in this dataset have been assigned a Government Ownership classification using the values "Federal", "State", "County Fee", "Tax Forfeit", or "Tribal" where it can be inferred from other fields in the parcel record. Only parcels from counties that have opted-in to sharing parcel data are included in this dataset. Fifty-six counties provided ownership content in the fields (owner_name, owner_more, tax_name, useclass1, and ownership) where ownership can be assigned to a parcel: Aitkin County, Anoka County, Becker County, Benton County, Big Stone County, Carlton County, Carver County, Cass County, County, Chippewa County, Chisago County, Clay County, Clearwater County, Cook County, Crow Wing County, Dakota County, Douglas County, Fillmore County, Grant County, Hennepin County, Houston County, Isanti County, Itasca County, Jackson County, Koochiching County, Lac qui Parle County, Lake County, Lake of the Woods County, Lyon County, Marshall County, McLeod County, Mille Lacs County, Mower County, Murray County, Norman County, Olmsted County, Otter Tail County, Pennington County, Pipestone County, Polk County, Pope County, Ramsey County, Red Lake County, Renville County, Scott County, Sherburne County, St. Louis County, Steele County, Stevens County, Traverse County, Wabasha County, Waseca County, Washington County, Wilkin County, Winona County, Wright County, and Yellow Medicine County. results.snippet: Parcel data has been identified as a foundational data layer for Minnesota and provides benefits for many operational uses. This dataset enables users to visualize the government owned parcels within each opt-in open county. It provides a best-effort inference of government ownership based on attributes provided by counties (often owner name, taxpayer name, or use class) where the ownership was not directly provided. This dataset was developed to enable geospatial professionals to perform statewide geospatial analysis, research, and mapping. For instance, knowing where government units have land holdings will help with coordinating land management and conservation efforts across Minnesota. The dataset provides a subset of the parcels from opt-in, open data counties, in a common coordinate system. Users can join this dataset to the open parcel dataset using the objectid field to access parcel attributes in the standard GAC schema.

results.title: Metropolitan 7-County Parcel Polygons - 2024
results.description:
This dataset includes all 7 metro counties that have made their parcel data freely available without a license or fees.

This dataset is a compilation of tax polygon layers assembled into a common coordinate system from Twin Cities, Minnesota metropolitan area counties. A standard set of attribute fields is included for each county. The attributes are the same for the polygon and points layers. Not all attributes are populated for all counties. The polygons are provided as individual county per sublayer/feature class.

NOTICE
The standard set of attributes changed to the MN Parcel Data Transfer Standard on 1/1/2019. https://www.mngeo.state.mn.us/committee/standards/parcel_attrib/parcel_attrib.html

Detailed information about the attributes can be found in the Metro Regional Parcel Attributes document.

This is a MetroGIS Regionally Endorsed dataset.

Comparison of parcel points to its polygon counterpart:
The polygon layer contains one record for each real estate/tax parcel polygon within each county's parcel dataset. Some counties have polygons for each individual condominium, and others do not. (See Completeness in Section 2 of the metadata for more information.) The points layer includes the same attribute fields as the polygon dataset. The points are intended to provide information in situations where multiple tax parcels are represented by a single polygon. One primary example of this is the condominium, though some counties stacked polygons for condos. Condominiums, by definition, are legally owned as individual, taxed real estate units. Records for condominiums may not show up in the polygon dataset. The points for the point dataset often will be randomly placed or stacked within the parcel polygon with which they are associated.

In many places a one-to-one relationship does not exist between these parcel polygons or points and the actual buildings or occupancy units that lie within them. There may be many buildings on one parcel and there may be many occupancy units (e.g. apartments, stores or offices) within each building. Additionally, no information exists within this dataset about residents of parcels. 

Additional information 
Additional information may be available from each county at the links listed below. Also, any questions or comments about suspected errors or omissions in this dataset can be addressed to the contact person at each individual county.

results.description:
This dataset includes all 7 metro counties that have made their parcel data freely available without a license or fees.

This dataset is a compilation of tax point layers assembled into a common coordinate system from Twin Cities, Minnesota metropolitan area counties. A standard set of attribute fields is included for each county. The attributes are the same for the polygon and points layers. Not all attributes are populated for all counties. The points are provided as individual county per sublayer/feature class.

NOTICE
The standard set of attributes changed to the MN Parcel Data Transfer Standard on 1/1/2019. https://www.mngeo.state.mn.us/committee/standards/parcel_attrib/parcel_attrib.html

Detailed information about the attributes can be found in the Metro Regional Parcel Attributes document.

This is a MetroGIS Regionally Endorsed dataset.

Comparison of parcel points to its polygon counterpart:
The polygon layer contains one record for each real estate/tax parcel polygon within each county's parcel dataset. Some counties have polygons for each individual condominium, and others do not. (See Completeness in Section 2 of the metadata for more information.) The points layer includes the same attribute fields as the polygon dataset. The points are intended to provide information in situations where multiple tax parcels are represented by a single polygon. One primary example of this is the condominium, though some counties stacked polygons for condos. Condominiums, by definition, are legally owned as individual, taxed real estate units. Records for condominiums may not show up in the polygon dataset. The points for the point dataset often will be randomly placed or stacked within the parcel polygon with which they are associated.

In many places a one-to-one relationship does not exist between these parcel polygons or points and the actual buildings or occupancy units that lie within them. There may be many buildings on one parcel and there may be many occupancy units (e.g. apartments, stores or offices) within each building. Additionally, no information exists within this dataset about residents of parcels.

results.title: Parcels, Compiled from Opt-In Open Data Counties, Minnesota
results.description:
This dataset is a compilation of county parcel data from Minnesota counties that have opted-in for their parcel data to be included in this dataset. It includes the following 59 counties that have opted-in as of the publication date of this dataset: Aitkin County, Anoka County, Becker County, Benton County, Big Stone County, Carlton County, Carver County, Cass County, Chippewa County, Chisago County, Clay County, Clearwater County, Cook County, Crow Wing County, Dakota County, Douglas County, Fillmore County, Grant County, Hennepin County, Houston County, Isanti County, Itasca County, Jackson County, Koochiching County, Lac qui Parle County, Lake County, Lake of the Woods County, Lyon County, Marshall County, McLeod County, Mille Lacs County, Morrison County, Mower County, Murray County, Norman County, Olmsted County, Otter Tail County, Pennington County, Pipestone County, Polk County, Pope County, Ramsey County, Red Lake County, Renville County, Rice County, Scott County, Sherburne County, St. Louis County, Stearns County, Steele County, Stevens County, Traverse County, Wabasha County, Waseca County, Washington County, Wilkin County, Winona County, Wright County, and Yellow Medicine County. If you represent a county not included in this dataset and would like to opt-in, please contact Heather Albrecht (Heather.Albrecht@hennepin.us), co-chair of the Minnesota Geospatial Advisory Council (GAC)’s Parcels and Land Records Committee's Open Data Subcommittee. County parcel data does not need to be in the GAC parcel data standard to be included. MnGeo will map the county fields to the GAC standard. County parcel data records have been assembled into a single dataset with a common coordinate system (UTM Zone 15) and common attribute schema. The county parcel data attributes have been mapped to the GAC parcel data standard for Minnesota: https://www.mngeo.state.mn.us/committee/standards/parcel_attrib/parcel_attrib.html This compiled parcel dataset was created using Python code developed by Minnesota state agency GIS professionals, and represents a best effort to map individual county source file attributes into the common attribute schema of the GAC parcel data standard. The attributes from counties are mapped to the most appropriate destination column. In some cases, the county source files included attributes that were not mapped to the GAC standard. Additionally, some county attribute fields were parsed and mapped to multiple GAC standard fields, such as a single line address. Each quarter, MnGeo provides a text file to counties that shows how county fields are mapped to the GAC standard. Additionally, this text file shows the fields that are not mapped to the standard and those that are parsed. If a county shares changes to how their data should be mapped, MnGeo updates the compilation. If you represent a county and would like to update how MnGeo is mapping your county attribute fields to this compiled dataset, please contact us. This dataset is a snapshot of parcel data, and the source date of the county data may vary. Users should consult County websites to see the most up-to-date and complete parcel data. There have been recent changes in date/time fields, and their processing, introduced by our software vendor. In some cases, this has resulted in date fields being empty. We are aware of the issue and are working to correct it for future parcel data releases. The State of Minnesota makes no representation or warranties, express or implied, with respect to the use or reuse of data provided herewith, regardless of its format or the means of its transmission. THE DATA IS PROVIDED “AS IS” WITH NO GUARANTEE OR REPRESENTATION ABOUT THE ACCURACY, CURRENCY, SUITABILITY, PERFORMANCE, MECHANTABILITY, RELIABILITY OR FITINESS OF THIS DATA FOR ANY PARTICULAR PURPOSE. This dataset is NOT suitable for accurate boundary determination. Contact a licensed land surveyor if you have questions about boundary determinations. DOWNLOAD NOTES: This dataset is only provided in Esri File Geodatabase and OGC GeoPackage formats. A shapefile is not available because the size of the dataset exceeds the limit for that format. The distribution version of the fgdb is compressed to help reduce the data footprint. QGIS users should consider using the Geopackage format for better results.

results.snippet: Parcel data has been identified as a foundational data layer for Minnesota and provides benefits for many operational uses. This dataset enables users to visualize the government owned parcels within each opt-in open county. It provides a best-effort inference of government ownership based on attributes provided by counties (often owner name, taxpayer name, or use class) where the ownership was not directly provided. This dataset was developed to enable geospatial professionals to perform statewide geospatial analysis, research, and mapping. For instance, knowing where government units have land holdings will help with coordinating land management and conservation efforts across Minnesota. The dataset provides a subset of the parcels from opt-in, open data counties, in a common coordinate system. Users can join this dataset to the open parcel dataset using the objectid field to access parcel attributes in the standard GAC schema.

This dataset is a compilation of address point data from metro area address authorities, which are predominantly cities. results.name: Anoka_County_1
results.title: Anoka County MN Covenants
results.description:
This layer shows racial covenants for Anoka County, Minnesota, produced by Mapping Prejudice, community mapmaking volunteers, and collaborators nationwide. This data set is maintained by Mapping Prejudice at the University of Minnesota Libraries. This data set is derived from reviewing millions of historic property records in counties across the United States. The property records were evaluated for the presence of racial covenants and mapped on to contemporary parcel maps.
 

Learn more about racial covenants, including how racial covenants continue to impact us today, from the Mapping Prejudice project at the University of Minnesota.

What are Racial Covenants?

Racial covenants are clauses that were inserted into property deeds to prevent people who were not White from buying or occupying land. Racial covenants can be found in the property records of every American community. They served as legally-enforceable contracts that stipulated that the property had to remain in the hands of White people. They ran with the land, which meant that it could be enforced in perpetuity. Anyone who dared to challenge this ban risked forfeiting their claim to the property.
 

Racial covenants were the brainchild of the real estate industry, which worked at the beginning of the 20th century with city planners to reshape the urban landscape. Animated by the desire to improve the environment of rapidly growing cities, they worked in tandem to promote parks; community gardens and playgrounds; municipal garbage collection; planned use commissions and zoning, which separated cities into different areas for industrial uses and residential life.
 

All of these efforts were guided by an urban planning orthodoxy founded on White supremacy. One of its central tenets was that mixed-race residential areas were hazardous and should be eliminated.

 

A note about using data across counties

Researchers should take care to avoid common pitfalls in analyzing historical data that may lead to confusion or misleading conclusions. For example, generally speaking, researchers should refrain from directly comparing one geography in these data to another without taking into account differences in the ways historical records were kept or preserved, differing histories of development over time, differences in geographic size between the communities, and differences in the urban or rural character of different geographies. 

 

Similarly, it’s important to remember that many populated areas today did not exist as populated areas when covenants were in place, and thus many contemporary populated areas did not have an opportunity to be covenanted. This means that calculating rates like “covenants per capita” or trying to determine what percentage of the geographic area was covenanted are not simple questions without taking into account what land was developed for residential use at the time covenants were in place or the contemporary populations.

 

What’s in the layers

Each feature in this dataset is a polygon that represents a modern parcel that has been linked to an original property record with a racial covenant. 

The fields are:

  • County (string) Name of the county
  • County FIPS Code (string) County 5-digit FIPS code
  • Document Number (string) Government document number of historical property deed
  • Covenant Date (string) Date the deed was executed 
  • Covenant Date (Date Format) (date) Generally, this is the date the deed or other document was executed.
    This is a date object that can be used to sort or symbolize by date.
  • Covenant Text (string) Text of racial covenant
  • Seller (string) Name of historical seller, also known as "grantor." 
  • Buyer (string) Name of historical buyer, also known as "grantee." 
  • Street Address (string) Street address of modern parcel match, according to county records.
  • City (string) City of modern parcel match, according to county records.
  • State (string) State
  • Zip (string) 5-digit ZIP of modern parcel match, according to county records.
  • Addition (string) Addition, also sometimes called subdivision or plat, listed in historical deed
  • Block (string) Block listed in historical deed
  • Lot (string) Lot number or range listed in historical deed
  • County PIN (string) Modern county parcel PIN. Not currently accurate, will be fixed in future exports.
  • Manual Correction (string) Whether or not a user has manually corrected the Zooniverse consensus output
  • Median Zooniverse Score (integer) Median Zooniverse consensus score, indicating how many users agreed precisely on various fields. Maximum is 1.0 for complete agreement.

About Mapping Prejudice

Mapping Prejudice is a team of historians, geographers, librarians, digital humanists and community activists seeking to expose structural racism. Our mission is to identify and map racial covenants, clauses that were inserted into property deeds to keep people who were not White from buying or occupying homes. From our base in the University of Minnesota Libraries, our interdisciplinary team collaborates with community members to expose the history of structural racism and support the work of reparations.

Data

Please note that these files are works in progress. Both the data and data formats are subject to change as we add covenants and refine our processes.

This data was pulled in April 2026. The most up-to-date data is available on the Mapping Prejudice GitHub. 

These files represent the covenants that have been successfully mapped and do not include unmapped covenants which have not yet been matched to modern properties.

These layers are data that Mapping Prejudice has gathered. There are other organizations across the United States that are also mapping racial covenants. 

Mapping these covenants takes months of work and is only possible if counties make their property records available for systematic analysis. Updated data and new counties will be added to this data set as they are available.
